subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE

subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: Question.

subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: that the Egyptian government has asserted that Egypt can order the United Nations emergency force out of the country whenever she wishes to do so. May I ask the Prime Minister whether the Canadian government agrees with the stand taken by the Egyptian government or whether it does not?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government does not agree with that stand taken by the Egyptian government. As I stated yesterday quite clearly-

subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext:
-the acquiescence of the Egyptian government was obtained for the stationing in Egyptian territory of an emergency force raised by the United Nations to do a certain job. It is our view-and this has been the view we have taken and expressed in New York- that if the Egyptian government wants to say that the job for which the consent was
[Mr. Sinclair.l

given has been completed, that should be communicated to the United Nations for its decision as to whether or not it agrees with the hypothetical assertion that the job has been completed.

subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: Well, in the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs last November, as reported at page 168 of Hansard of November 29, 1956, part of the job of the United Nations emergency force-

subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: Question.

subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE

-was described as being:

Now, does the Canadian government still believe that is one of the functions of the United Nations emergency force?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think we should have a debate at this time. That statement was made and is on the record, and has not been withdrawn.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister supplementary to his exchanges with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. In view of some of the press interpretations that have been placed on what the Prime Minister said yesterday with regard to the situation in the Suez, will he make it clear to the house and the country as to what he meant when he referred to the possibility of the use of force to overcome resistance? Was he referring to collective action by the United Nations or to action by individual nations on their own?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker; I was not referring to collective action by the United Nations. I thought I made it quite clear that the United Nations effort was all directed to preventing the resumption of the use of force in that area. What I was pointing out in answer to the question that had been put was that the only alternative to obtaining the acquiescence of the government of the area where the force was to be placed would be a resumption of the use of force, and I was putting it forward as an indication that the United Nations had no other method but that of trying to prevail upon the governments interested to follow the courses indicated by the views accepted by a majority of the United Nations in the resolutions adopted.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question. Does the Prime Minister think the situation in the Suez has

reached a point where even such a possibility should be suggested by one such as the Prime Minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not suggesting anything. I thought I was pointing out to the house that that was an alternative that could not be considered. Therefore when the words "Is the whole thing subject to the whim of Mr. Nasser?" are used, there is no other way of obtaining the acquiescence of the governments concerned that can be resorted to unless fighting is to flare up again in that region.

subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a supplementary question. How does the Prime Minister tie in his statement today with the statement he made last November to the effect that once Egypt had given consent for this force to go into the area, then Egypt had no further control, that it was then up to the United Nations?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: I think I made it quite clear that the position of a great many members of the United Nations, including Canada, is that once the consent was given to the stationing of United Nations forces there, the relationship of the forces is only with the United Nations, and that if the government of Egypt wishes any change made, the course would be for it to signify its wishes to the United Nations for a decision of the United Nations. As far as we know, the commander has been appointed by the United Nations and takes his directions from the United Nations.

subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: But are those decisions not being left to the Secretary General of the United Nations, and not to the military commander at all?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: These are matters that are being dealt with by the United Nations, and it does not change the way in which they will be dealt with by the United Nations to have the hon. gentleman direct questions to me, and for me to answer those questions.

subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: Has the Secretary General of the United Nations not taken the stand with regard to that question that it can do nothing without the consent of Egypt?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext:
The Secretary General of the United Nations has taken the stand that he obtained the consent of Egypt once, and that no further consent was required.
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Calgary North, in connection with the discussion of the reconnaissance unit which is going forward to the United Nations emergency force, asked this question:
Did Egypt give its consent to sending these new troops . . . ?
Mr. Speaker, the request for these troops was made by the secretary general to the government of Canada after consultation by him with the commanding general of the United Nations emergency force. No consultation with the government of Egypt by the secretary general or any agent of the secretary general was required or took place, as there was no question of Egypt's consent being necessary.

subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs arising out of the answer he gave that permission was not required for the extra Canadian troops sent to the United Nations emergency force. Can the minister tell the house how long the force would be able to remain in Egypt if Egypt directed that the force be withdrawn forthwith?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I could not answer that question, nor do I think anyone could.

subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Can the minister tell the house of any provisions in the United Nations charter or otherwise whereby the force could legally remain on the territory of a sovereign state if that state requested the force to withdraw, under the present system?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext:
I cannot, Mr. Speaker, give a legal opinion, but of course when the United Nations forces are in any country by agreement, the rights of sovereignty of that country have to be accepted and respected.
In the case of Egypt those sovereign rights which have been respected have to be considered within United Nations action, within the United Nations assembly resolution which Egypt agreed to for the introduction of that force to do certain tasks.

subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. In the event that Egypt should request the withdrawal of those troops would Israel not be consulted

Inquiries of the Ministry in any way, as to whether they should be withdrawn from the Gaza strip?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Secretary General of the United Nations has indicated, and a great many delegates have agreed with this view of the case, that if Egypt at any time makes any request for the withdrawal of the United Nations force, the request should first go to the advisory committee of the assembly which has been set up. It would be discussed there between the secretary general and the advisory committee, and the advisory committee could then refer the matter to the full assembly, which would take whatever action it could and which was required.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: Is the Secretary of State for External Affairs now in a position to answer the question which I directed to him a few days ago, and which the Minister of Fisheries said he would refer to him, regarding the continental shelf? Is the application going forward in the United Nations for international recognition of the 12-mile limit for Canadian control of this continental shelf, and does this application include all resources in that continental shelf?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secreiary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
This question of the legal position of the continental shelf and territorial waters is now, as my hon. friend knows, under discussion at the United Nations assembly and at the international law commission which has been set up by the United Nations.
One of the recommendations of the international law commission, that is the body which has been studying these matters, is that the coastal state should be recognized as exercising over the continental shelf sovereign rights for the purpose of exploring and exploiting its natural resources. This particular recommendation, along with all other recommendations relating to the laws of the sea, including the breadth of territorial waters, will be considered by an international conference which the general assembly has recommended should be convened in March, 1958, a year from now. Canada, of course, will be represented at this conference. In the meantime, preparations are being made by an interdepartmental committee to make recommendations to the government as to what position should be adopted.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED REQUEST FOR CANADIAN FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister if the Canadian government has been asked to extend financial assistance to Ghana, and if so, what decision the Canadian government has taken on the request?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REPORTED REQUEST FOR CANADIAN FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I saw the Gazette this morning I anticipated that there might be such a question, but I was engaged in a council meeting which lasted until 1.30, and it was only when 1 returned from lunch that I obtained some information about what had taken place.
There has been no request for financial assistance, but there was a debate in the House of Commons at Westminster on November 30 concerning the practicability of suggesting the establishment of a commonwealth development corporation that would consider development projects in former colonies that grew into the status of dominions and were no longer in the position where they could receive advice and assistance from the United Kingdom colonial development corporation. There were suggestions made that there might be a commonwealth development corporation comprising all the member nations of the commonwealth. Another suggestion was that there might be a commonwealth bank for the purpose of making funds available for development purposes.
On January 24 there was a debate along similar lines in the House of Lords. No request was made by the United Kingdom government, but the high commissioner communicated to our Department of External Affairs copies of the Hansard of the House of Commons and the House of Lords, and asked for an expression of our views concerning the practicability of the suggestions that had been made by private members to the United Kingdom government in that respect.

Mr. Speaker, I feel I should explain to the house that part of the answer I gave yesterday to the hon. member for Nanaimo was incomplete and, I regret to say, inaccurate.
It had slipped my mind that in the revision of the immigration regulations made during the course of last year it had been provided that immigrants from the United Kingdom,

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 28
and March 5 the hon. member for Colchester-Hants (Mr. Purdy) asked about the possibility of extending the provisions of the maritime marshland rehabilitation program

to certain other lands in the maritime provinces. I have had the question examined, and find that the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act restricts the program to the construction of dikes, aboiteaux and other protective works which have for their purpose the protection of the marshland from the sea. speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, but I did not hear what the hon. member said.
I was wondering whether the minister intended to continue the review he was giving last night. If not, I should like to make some remarks.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I intended to continue, Mr. Chairman, but I am not one to stop my own estimates from passing. However, I might continue with the remarks I started making yesterday. When the discussion terminated yesterday at six o'clock, I had been analysing some of the comments on the postage stamps issued by the department, and I gave what I intended to be an adequate answer to some of the questions asked by the hon. member for Kootenay West. To those comments I should like to add the fact that the advance orders for the outdoor recreation issue have been increasingly heavy. It would seem that public acceptance of these stamps has been highly favourable, both in Canada and in the United States, where it is hoped they will serve a useful purpose in promoting tourist travel to this country.
Some hon. members-I think it was the hon. member for Lambton West and the hon. member for Lambton-Kent-suggested that a postage stamp design be issued to commemorate the one hundredth anniversary of the discovery of petroleum in Canada. I wish to tell them that proposals have been received for the issuing of such a stamp and that the matter is now under consideration by the department and the government.

The hon. member for Saint John made comment with regard to the type and quality of stamps issued by the department. During the discussion in committee last year and again yesterday I explained briefly what was the policy which had been followed. It is quite true that from 1950 on there was a departure from the procedure previously used for the manufacture of stamps and it may account, to some extent, for the different type of picture that now appears on the stamps.
Up to that time the stamps were made from composite photographs, and the engraver would make a copy of the composite photograph. From 1950 on it was thought that stamps should be used to encourage art in this country and that we should ask leading Canadian artists who would be interested in providing designs for stamps to do so. That has been the procedure followed since 1950. Hence the engraver preparing the plate to manufacture a stamp actually copies an artistic design-that is, an artist's conception of what the stamp is to depict-rather than what was a composite photograph which possibly would be more precise in many instances.
There is nothing to prevent us from going back to the other method. I think possibly a mixture of the two methods would be very good. That is my own opinion, although I am not a philatelist. I believe that in the issue of postage stamps there is a field in which the talents of our Canadian artists can be used.
In that connection may I just ask whether the department is considering a type of artistic design other than this abstract art for our stamps of the future?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Of course we ask artists to make the design. I suppose one opinion as to the value of one particular artist's work as compared with that of another is a fairly personal thing. I can assure the hon. member that the men whom we have asked to provide some of these designs-for instance, they are men like the late Emanuel Hahn of Toronto, A. L. Pollock of Toronto, Lawrence Hyde of Ottawa, A. A. Beament of Montreal and a few others-all leading Canadian artists. Furthermore, after the design has been conceived by the artist and has been submitted to us, we in turn submit that design to experts from the national gallery in order to have their assurance that artistically it is correct. When the design depicts a particular subject-for instance, I am thinking of our animal designs- we submit the design to an expert zoologist to make sure that from the technical side the design is correct.

Has the minister ever considered letting these designs be made by way
Supply-Post Office
of competition among artists in order to procure the best out of several?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Yes; that was done originally. I am told that when we started this policy of asking Canadian artists to provide designs, competitions were arranged, but it was found that this procedure did not attract the best artists. In other words it was found that the really leading artists were fairly busy in their own fields, and that they might be interested in providing designs for the post office if they were commissioned to do so but that they would not participate in a competition. I am speaking only from memory. I believe about the only leading Canadian artist who competed was Mr. Hahn, to whom I have already referred.
But in this kind of competition we would get every type of sketch from that of the Grade VI school child to some amateur artist, and the work involved did not justify continuing the procedure. From then on the department proceeded to commission artists directly to furnish individual designs.

I have had complaints from a great number of people, especially from people who are partially blind and from elderly people.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That is correct, Mr. Chairman. We have received complaints about some of the stamps which have been issued in past years, and we have asked that in future designs the denominations of the stamps should appear more clearly.

Would it be
possible to try to keep the different denominations in one colour as much as possible, or, perhaps, in one or two colours.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs

May I ask the minister why
it is that up till now, as far as Vancouver is concerned, the postal officials who worked overtime during Christmas still have not got their overtime cheques? May I ask why it has taken so long? I got a letter only today about this; it is on my desk now. There was a notice posted saying that the post office was "broke" or words to that effect, and still they have not got their Christmas overtime cheques. It is now March. How long have these people to wait until they get the money they earned last December?

Supply-Post Office

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I am told it is being paid
right now. What did happen is this: Overtime is not paid by the department, under overtime regulations, until the 1st of February. That is there is a regulation which provides that Christmas overtime shall be paid in cash only in the month following J anuary, and only to the extent that this overtime has not been liquidated by leave. What has happened in actual practice is that 95 per cent of the overtime is paid in cash. That has been true for the last four or five years, at any rate, and I think it was the same before-not more than 5 per cent of this overtime was liquidated in leave during the month of January. But only after the termination of January can we get ready to pay that overtime. Naturally this is done through the central pay office, and the regular salary cheques have to be processed before action is taken, so there is some delay during the month of February before the overtime pay reaches the employees.
I am told that what did happen in this particular case was that when they got toward the end of issuing the cheques for overtime they found that the amount allotted for overtime had been expended. Then we had to go through the procedure of transferring funds, which requires an approval of treasury board; it means you have to go through the process of making a submission to the treasury board, and have that approved before authority is given to us to issue these cheques. That is what happened in Vancouver.

I appreciate the apology the
minister has made, but I am referring not to carriers but to clerks.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It is the same thing.

As a matter of fact there
was a notice posted on the boards of the Vancouver post offices to the effect that they could not pay in money. I have a copy here, and I will quote it. It says: "We have exhausted our funds and therefore the cheques will not be issued."
I have a number of notices on the subject. I accept the apology of the minister on behalf of the post office employees, but it is now March. I got a letter this morning by airmail from Vancouver, and these men have still not received their cheques for last December.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot add anything to what I have said. I am informed that this overtime is in the process of being paid. I wish to tell the hon. member, however, that the explanation I gave applies to all employees he mentioned. I have no doubt, if the hon. member has received a letter of
complaint saying that the cheque has not been handed over yet, that it must be true; the letter must have come through with a very short delay because, as the hon. member knows, the mail service between Vancouver and Ottawa is rapid.
I would like to know if you will pay interest on your delayed cheques in the same way as the government charges us interest on anything we owe the government.

That is an intelligent
question.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I have a few other comments I wish to make, and I wonder if the hon. member would mind if I answered specific questions on the other items later, as there were many questions asked? I would prefer to do that.
Referring, now, to the general discussion, Mr. Chairman, I would like to deal with the remarks made by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace regarding the postal union congress which I stated is to open in Ottawa on August 14, 1957, that is, this summer. I may be wrong, but it would appear from the remarks of the hon. member that possibly he has not a complete appreciation of the magnitude of this undertaking nor of the extended period of the congress. I have stated that some 96 countries will be represented by delegates, and that the period of the congress will extend from the 14th of August to, certainly, the end of September or the early part of October. When the arrangements were being prepared the indications were that the number of delegates attending would be approximately 350, but the latest information would indicate that this number may be increased.
The hon. member seemed to have the impression that the amount to be provided by this estimate for this universal congress was to furnish lavish entertainment to the delegates. This is, of course, not the case. Included in the facilities for which the estimate provides, Mr. Chairman, is the payment for the installation of a simultaneous translation system into four languages which is to be installed here in parliament.
I might point out here that while Canada provides for this service and the cost is included in these estimates the greater part of the amount involved is to be recovered from the universal postal union's international bureau at Berne. Similarly, while Canada

is assisting in the provision of the necessary staff requirements for the operation of the congress, the international bureau at Berne will reimburse Canada for the amount involved in the salaries paid to Canadian employees whose services are used by the international bureau's secretariat during the operation of the congress.
I must point out here that those employees of the Post Office Department who may be working at the congress and who are already classified employees will simply be assigned to that work and will not be receiving any additional pay. Therefore their salaries will not be reimbursed by the international bureau. But the salaries of the clerical help, messengers, other staff and so on that will be required for the operation of the congress, which salaries will be paid from these estimates, are to be reimbursed by the international bureau after the congress has terminated.
I might point out that sessions of the congress are held somewhat along the lines of United Nations meetings, with which most hon. members are familiar. The work is distributed to a certain number of committees, as a matter of fact to nine committees in this case. There is a tremendous amount of printing similar to what takes place in the case of United Nations committee meetings. There is a report of the discussions in committee and in the general meetings in the same way as at the United Nations. It is not quite as elaborate a report as we have in Hansard in that it is not verbatim but it calls for the hiring of rapporteurs and the clerical staff necessary to produce this documentation for the next day of the meeting. Therefore the work involved is considerable but, as I have pointed out, the cost of a large part of it is eventually reimbursed by the international bureau.
With regard to the matter of hospitality, I can assure hon. members that it will be far from lavish, certainly compared with the hospitality which I am told has been extended to delegates to previous congresses held in other countries. In the main it will consist of a short visit to Montreal and Quebec and another to Toronto and Niagara Falls for the purpose of letting the delegates see some of the representative parts of Canada without going too far afield and at the same time getting them away from Ottawa so that the congress officials can catch up with the revising of proposals and preparation of the agreements for signature at the end of the meeting. If I go into some length on this matter it is in order to leave no doubt in the mind of anyone that this is indeed a hard working group engaged in a very essential task of far-reaching importance.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North raised a question about the establishment of a postal station in the municipality of East Kildonan, but I notice the hon. member is out of the house at the present time so perhaps I will leave this point until later in the afternoon when he returns.
There was a matter raised by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich which I think I can discuss briefly at this time. It concerned the responsibility of the Post Office Department in connection with the provision of postal services to the armed services. He referred particularly to the camp at Shilo and to the new camp at Gagetown. He said that he had received complaints that the postal service in these camps was slower than it was in the adjoining municipalities. Here I must explain that with regard to the delivery of mail to military camps or air force stations, any military establishment, either of two systems exists.
If it is a closed camp, that is, a camp where only military personnel live and train and no civilians are admitted to the camp or live within its boundaries, then the mail to that air force station or military camp goes to the nearest civilian post office and is delivered by that post office to personnel of the postal corps who in turn bring it to the camp and have the responsibility for the sortation and distribution of mail within the camp. In the other camps where there is civilian personnel, where there are wives and dependents of service personnel or civilian employees, we do operate a post office within the boundary of the camp and the mail is taken to it in the regular fashion from the nearest civilian post office. In the case of the camp post office, if I may describe it as such, all service mail is delivered in bulk by that postmaster to the service personnel, to the postal corps people, and they again are responsible for the sortation and the distribution of that service mail, and our own post office serves the civilian people. Therefore if there are delays in the delivery of mail to service personnel within these service establishments, I must say that I do not believe the responsibility can rest on the employees of the Post Office Department.

In the case of Gagetown, is there an army post office in the new town of Oromocto?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: What is proposed there-I understand Oromocto is to be set up as a town under provincial statute-is that there will be a federal building in which will be a civilian post office. The civilian post office will serve the wives and dependents and civilian employees of the camp. The service mail will be delivered in bulk from that civilian post office to the postal corps people who in turn will make the sortation and distribution amongst service personnel.
That will be separate and apart from the post office?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It will come from the same post office but all service mail will be delivered in bulk to the postal corps people.

I just wanted to ask this question. There is a village of Oromocto there now, and then there will be this separate town of Oromocto perhaps a mile away. Will you still retain the post office at the village and have another post office at the new town that is going to be built?

speechtext: I understand that is correct, yes. If I may suggest, Mr. Chairman, unless hon. members have other questions to direct to me now, possibly the first item can carry and I would answer the other inquiries I would receive on the specific items. It is immaterial to me.

I do not care whether the minister answers this question now or if he wishes to proceed, but I am not sure it comes under operations. What is the policy of the department, or does it have an overall policy, with regard to employees of the post office department accepting other employment outside of their working hours? If there is a policy, does it stipulate that they shall accept only certain types of employment?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The employees of the postal department can accept-and in fact quite a few do, I believe-employment outside but they cannot accept it if at any time it interferes with their own work or their working hours. In their free time they can accept such employment, and as I have said quite a number of them do.

I am sorry I do not have with me a letter which came to me just recently. It is in my office but I can give the gist of it to the Postmaster General. The local postmaster inquired into the activities of a member, and according to this statement the postmaster felt that the man's

health might be affected. I have not the full particulars, but according to the man the money which he made outside of regular post office employment would not indicate enough time would be consumed to affect his health. The letter from the postmaster rather read as though this was a periodic checkup. Do you have periodic checkups on the employees?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I think I should have
qualified my previous statement by saying that employees are required to ask permission to work outside. Of course, each case is looked into individually and in some cases-I do not know what the case is to which the hon. member refers but I will be glad to look into it-it might be that a man worked on a particular shift and we happen to know he is not in very good health as indicated by his attendance record or sick leave record.
