I did not hear all the minister's answers to questions, but the other day I mentioned the regulation fixing four boxes to the mile for rural mail service. I pointed out to the minister that this is working great hardship on people living in rural districts, especially where quite a number of farmers are leaving the district. There are not as many people required on the farms now, and they are combining farms-that sort of thing. I wonder if the department is considering relaxing this regulation and giving mail service to the people of the country districts?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, I do not believe the actual regulations have been changed but certainly their application has been changed. A more flexible approach has been adopted. There are many cases where, under particular circumstances, we have relaxed the rule of four boxes to the mile. Routes have been granted where there were three boxes, particularly when certain adjustments have become necessary because of a change in a route or an extension of service. As I say, the department has relaxed the application of that regulation.
We have not noticed it particularly.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that the point he is raising receives my deep sympathy because I am sure I have twice as many rural routes in my constituency as he has.
I wonder if these instructions have gone out to all the district inspectors in every part of Canada, to relax these regulations?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Actually, there have been no instructions sent out to the district inspectors because the procedure that is followed in the establishment of a new route or for an extension, is that the inspector is asked to report on the proposed route and the decision as to whether the route should be established, and the length of the route, is taken here. In actual practice, therefore, the application of the regulation is done at headquarters.
But the district inspector's recommendation is taken into consideration.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: He reports, makes a sketch of the rural route and indicates where the proposed boxes are to be and what the length of the route is, as well as what his own recommendation would be.
That is a step in the right direction.

I wonder if the minister can help me with a new problem that faces, I think, the whole metropolitan area of Toronto. It deals with the designation of individual area names for postal delivery. I have been in touch with the minister about this before, but I have not had the benefit of a complete answer. Apparently, there must be some reason behind the department designating individual area names in connection with the department's distribution methods.
This policy has had some serious repercussions for business men in those areas. First of all, I want to say that no one is objecting to the names that are used because, of course, they represent the areas in which people live and of which they are quite proud. But I believe that most of the people in this rapidly expanding metropolitan area are desirous of having a Toronto district number put at the end of their business address.
The reasons for this, from the businessman's point of view, are fairly important. They have a letterhead and if they use a Toronto business address it indicates to their customers, whoever they are dealing with, that this is the place of their business. If an individual district name is used it might be difficult to find out just where it is in the ordinary course in checking maps, and so forth. In addition, sir, I think our freight tariff classifications do not carry these individual postal district names, and as a result it is most difficult in dealing with freight traffic matters.
I have been informed as well that the banks use these place name designations as a differential in connection with their charges for the exchange fee on their cheques. In other words, within the area proper of Toronto we
Supply-Post Office
may have one rate apply, and within the total metropolitan area we may have a larger amount apply in so far as the bank is concerned. I understand this is done pretty well, because of the place name designation by the-Post Office Department.
I have been led to believe that this system is, to a great extent, based on a plan for sorting of material probably on its way into Toronto, and relieving to some extent the major postal office in Toronto from some of the sorting work. Is it a greater strain, is it more difficult on the man doing the sorting job before the mail reaches Toronto, to put to one side the Toronto postal designation, Toronto 21, in lieu of, say, a place name-designation such as Scarborough, Rexdale,, or a designation of that sort? It seems to me it would require no greater mental capacity, and surely experienced men could make that distribution in that manner and see that the mail for those districts goes to the subpostal delivery base without having a special place name which brings in all this additional inconvenience to business people.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Well, the point which has just been raised by the hon. member brings in many more problems than I think he fully appreciates. In fact, some of the criticism which the department and I have received was to the effect that in certain parts of the country we had attempted to do exactly what my hon. friend suggests, and that instead of using old names of localities we were attempting to impose a numerical system based on the central office. This problem is brought about by the expansion of our larger cities, and it becomes a question of distribution and sortation, as the hon. member pointed out. An attempt was made. We simply asked the cooperation of businessmen and of householders generally to use numbers to divide, say, the Toronto metropolitan area, into a certain number of districts, each bearing a number. The postal address would be such and such a street, Toronto 7 or Toronto 8. Well, it has never been possible, except as regards some business people, to get the co-operation of the public. In fact, each time a new area was brought in to the metropolitan district, like Rexdale or Scarborough, for instance, the complaint was, "now, this locality has always been called Rexdale; it has always been called Scarborough, and this is how we know it and we do not want simply to have a number to describe our locality." It is necessary to use either one or the other because, with the expansion of our great centres, there is a limit to the memory of our sorters. They can remember a certain number; they can remember a certain number of streets in a city; but

Supply-Post Office
it becomes limited after that. When you reach that limit there is a breakdown.
Furthermore, as new areas are attached to a main city there is a duplication in the names of streets. You will have two streets, two avenues bearing the same name, and unless the exact locality is described by either a local name or a zone number you will have some mis-addressed letters. Delivery is delayed and the letter may go to the wrong address. The hon. member referred to Rexdale. I can think of a few other places. The fact that we do ask the addressee to use the name of the locality does not prevent adding the word "Toronto". In other words, a letter addressed to someone at Rexdale, Toronto, would be properly addressed and there is nothing to prevent anyone from doing so.

Mr. Chairman, I was most interested in getting that explanation because I think there are many people who do not understand that in these cases they can put "Toronto" on their letterhead and expect delivery.
I might suggest one thing to the minister. I was very careful when I made my remarks about not indicating that people were not satisfied with those names, but there is a great deal of difference in names and in this new expansion we are going to have a lot of subdividers' names which have no historical basis in the constituencies that we represent. On the other hand, there are some that are very well known. Certainly, in my own constituency, if you mentioned Islington you would find that it is well-known. It has been there; it is a place with quite a history. The department might take that into consideration and when we start to designate those areas make a differentiation between those which happen to be the result of a subdivision new name and those which have a name which is a carryover.
I think the minister has answered the one thing that was left in my mind in connection with Toronto because I was going to ask him this question. If someone addressed a letter to one of these new areas and did not put the individual designation on it but used the term "Toronto" only, would that letter get to its destination? I think the minister is going to answer yes, which proves to me that an awful lot of this mail is going through the main postal office in any case. I am just wondering whether the new designations are always entirely necessary but at the same time I am very happy to know that I can advise people to use the second designation as well.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I might add to my previous remarks by saying that in the

choice of these names it has been the practice of the department since we adopted this procedure to consult with the municipal authorities on the choice of the postal name that should be used in our postal distribution system.
As regards his second question, it is quite possible that a letter addressed as he suggested would get to the destination in the normal period of time but the chances are that it would have to be redirected to a directory office and that, although it would eventually be delivered, it would be delivered after a few days' delay.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to delay the committee unduly but I think I did ask the minister a couple of questions on March 1. In the course of his answers in the past few days he has answered at least one of them with respect to the kind of postage stamps for the centennial year.
One of the questions I asked him had to do with the slide in the mountain regions of British Columbia and the delay in getting mail through the Fraser valley to the city. I gave him notice of that question some time ago on the orders of the day. He was going to investigate but we have not received a report as yet.
The other question, which I wish he would elaborate on because it may result in my not having to discuss it any further in the house, has to do with the parcel post carriers in the metropolitan area of New Westminster. If the minister would be in a position to speak about this matter for a few moments I would be pleased.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with regard to the first question my hon. friend raised concerning the delay brought about by a slide in the Fraser valley some time during the month of February, I did at the time answer the hon. member to the effect that local postal authorities have full authority whenever an emergency arises to take whatever means are available to see that the mail gets through. Usually this is done through the use of a different motor vehicle service or a different route if the usual means of conveyance has been stopped.
In the case of Hope to which he referred the truck service which was to carry the mail was scheduled to leave at 6.45 in the morning. The slide took place and after inquiries were made it was found that the mail would be able to get through the next morning and that would be the best way of continuing the service rather than trying to improvise a service, and that is what took place.

The hon. member also asked me questions with reference to parcel post delivery in certain parts of New Westminster and Vancouver. In New Westminster up to this time parcel post delivery had been done by six individual contractors each operating individually on a temporary arrangement. They were not under any formal contract with the department and had in fact only an arrangement with the department confirmed by a letter. All except one entered into the temporary arrangement in 1955 and the sixth entered into a similar temporary arrangement in 1956.
Before the minister continues perhaps he would answer another question. Several of these contractors had a permanent arrangement up to 1955, had they not?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: None of these gentlemen had been under contract with the Post Office Department before that time. They had worked for another contractor who was doing the work and they were hired as drivers. In 1955, as I mentioned, that contractor gave up his contract and the department made a temporary arrangement with each individual driver to continue servicing the route they were already servicing under terms which were agreed upon between the two parties. None of these men had ever been classified employees of the department and had never received any pay as an employee of the department.
The only time they were actually under contract with the department itself was from 1955 to the date of termination?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
That is correct and it was on a temporary arrangement which they had agreed could be terminated at any time on the part of either of the two parties to the agreement. What happened there is that after making a postal area of Vancouver we found we had to rearrange the whole system of delivery with regard to letter delivery, parcel post delivery, special letter delivery, C.O.D. delivery and so on. We found that within the area we were operating through 14 individual contractors similar to these. Some of them were working on an hourly basis agreed upon with the department and others were working on a per item basis. With a view to making it a more economical and efficient operation and experimenting on an over-all per item basis we advised the gentlemen to whom my hon. friend referred that their agreement would terminate at a certain time. As I have stated, the idea was to operate throughout the entire Vancouver postal area on a per item basis. Each of these gentlemen was offered an opportunity
Supply-Post Office
to continue doing that work but as an employee of the new contractor.
I know my hon. friend is particularly interested in the conditions of work which were offered to these people and I think I can now describe the terms of employment to him. I think the hon. member will agree with me that the conditions which were offered are better than the conditions under which they are now working.
The proposed terms of employment stated that the wages would be scheduled on a per item basis within the districts involved but always subject to the guarantee that the prevailing wage scale would be met. At the present time the rate is $1.74 per hour. In other words, that is the minimum which they could earn. Further, they would be provided with workmen's compensation board coverage which they do not have now and also with unemployment insurance coverage which they do not have at the present time. They would also have received within the first year a paid annual vacation of one week-that is in 1957-and two weeks from then on. They would also be paid for statutory holidays according to the terms of the union and would have had contributory group life insurance. They would no longer have to bother about ownership and insurance coverage for their vehicles and would be provided with the uniforms and equipment necessary to do the work.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister for this lucid explanation. I will leave that topic now and ask him if he would have his departmental officials examine into the problem of the four cent letter rate with respect to the district of South Westminster which I raised earlier in the discussion. I think on further consideration they might find it desirable to include this in the metropolitan area?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That survey is being made just now.

Mr. Chairman, I find that, if you wait long enough, most of the information in which you are interested comes out. However, I wish to make a few remarks at this time. I was very much interested yesterday when the Postmaster General began his remarks and said that he was sympathetic to the rural areas. I am chiefly interested in the rural mail delivery. I have not any great problem. There are several things about which I could speak but I believe that the officials in my district are endeavouring to improve the rural mail delivery as a matter of policy. However, I should like to supplement some of the remarks that have been made.

Supply-Post Office
I think that some attention should be given to the matter of trying to work out a policy in order to give the country people more nearly daily mail than they are getting at the present time. I know there are not too many three deliveries a week in my constituency. There are a few. Those people keep after everyone. They feel that if cities are going to get two deliveries a day-and they read about it-they should get at least one delivery a day. They are living in the country, they are isolated to some extent and their daily newspaper and their reading material are quite important to them.
There is another thing I should like to mention. I believe that the department are doing this to some extent now in their surveys. I believe more and more routes could be amalgamated and worked out in the country so that with good roads, ploughed roads in the winter and all that, you could fairly well arrive shortly at the place where country people might get daily mail and you could cut out this system of two deliveries and three deliveries a week. I think it is something that should be seriously considered before too much attention is given to better deliveries in the city.
My experience has been-and I appreciate it greatly-that the department are not now so sticky about these three boxes and four boxes per mile. I find that they are ready to consider the area. I appreciate that fact.
There is one other thing that I should like to say. I was in the area that was affected by the railroad strike and I want to compliment the officials who made the arrangements in my area. There is an area of some 175 miles in which the mail was all delivered by train. It all had to be rearranged. The postmaster and his staff in my own home town in my opinion deserve a great deal of credit for the way in which the mail was handled. It was a sort of centre to which the mail came from both ends. It all had to be re-sorted and then sent out. I do not know whether or not that staff would get any extra consideration in the way of pay. In any event, they deserve a word of commendation. As far as I know, the change went into effect very smoothly. While our mails were held up for an hour or two, everybody seemed to feel that it was still a job well done.
I should like to bring another matter to the attention of the department. Maybe the minister can tell me something about it. The mail has gone back in the regular channels of carriage-that is through the trains- through which it went formerly, I understand. But for the last four or five weeks we have not been getting the service through from

central Canada down home that we were getting formerly, as far as deliveries are concerned. I will give you some personal experience. Mail that was mailed some time on Monday to my town did not arrive until Tiiursday or Friday; mail that was mailed on Tuesday would arrive sooner. There has been a good deal of hold up. There may be a reason for it. It is not owing to poor addressing. It is not owing to the local post office mail being held up. It is not owing to a great deal of mail. We cannot quite understand it. Whether part of the mail goes by air to Fredericton and is then transferred and part of it goes by train and is transferred, I do not know. Maybe there is an explanation. Maybe the matter will straighten itself out. It just seems to be something that, after the strike was over, has not been going as regularly and as well as it was going before. As a matter of fact, it has not been going as well as when the strike was on. I just bring this matter to the attention of the minister. It is not too serious but it is something that is rather peculiar. It may be that there is an ungreased cog in the machinery some place and that the matter will straighten itself out.
In the last report available I notice, with respect to insurance, the amount that it has cost the department for indemnity payments and so on. I should like to ask the minister for an explanation. I do not just quite understand it. It is found at page 23 of the report. I notice there that for registered and domestic mail, the amount of indemnity paid was $1,865 from departmental funds and I notice the same thing throughout. Does that mean there are losses in respect of registered mail that must be made good by the department? Does it refer to lost letters and is it covered by insurance? Why is something paid from the departmental funds? Then it says "Indemnity Recovered". Would that be from insurance companies or what? I should like to have from the minister a word of explanation.
I think that nearly everything else that I had in mind has been fairly well covered and I am not going to take up any more time.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I wish to thank my hon.
friend for his remarks, particularly with regard to extensions of rural mail service. I must say that I am quite in agreement with him. Generally speaking, I think that policy has been followed during the course of the last year and that we have many more areas where there is six times a week delivery of rural mail than existed before. Of course he must understand that there are still areas where the road conditions are very bad and where those in the distance between each pair of boxes, or in other words the number of patrons in the distance covered, is very

small indeed. But inasmuch as rearrangement can be made, our policy is to do it and to try to extend rural mail service to as many people in the country as possible.
With regard to his complaint that he is experiencing some delay in the receipt of his mail coming from central Canada, I think he said that the service was poor; I take it that he meant it was poor as compared with the situation that existed during the strike.
And previously.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Of course, during the period of the strike we replaced most of those services which were provided by the railroad by truck services, by motor vehicle services. One of the advantages of motor vehicle services over the trains is that we can schedule its departure in order to meet our deadline after sortation whereas in the case of the trains we have to make use of the trains according to the schedules set by the company. In many cases it could be that because of the use of the truck service mail would get between one point and another and be delivered in quicker time, because it might arrive there in time for the sortation to take place and go out on the first delivery. I think that might be the explanation in this case. However, we are making a survey at the present time as a result of our experience of all these rules.

With regard to rural delivery, may I tell the minister that in some parts of the country where there used to be two or three farms along a route, today one man often owns that land, and there will only be one mail box in a distance of a mile and a half where you used to have two or three. That is the case in my constituency, and I think it is not an isolated situation. But it must be remembered that the one farmer concerned is doing more business. He is farming that land, and I think that must be taken into consideration with regard to the rural route arrangements.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I quite agree. I will give the hon. member a further explanation when we get on to operations.

Mr. Chairman, when I last spoke on the subject of these estimates I said I intended to make some further observations. I had thought to make some remarks about stamps, but this subject seems to have been thoroughly covered by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert. The comments I had in mind were along the lines of those made by the hon. member for Kootenay West about the symbolic way in which these stamps are designed and presented each year. Of course, I do not think the department is producing the stamps with
Supply-Post Office
the particular idea I have in mind, but they do run in a kind of pattern. The first depicted a goose, and I claimed the government was killing the goose that laid the "golden egg", or the revenue which came from it. I asked if they had it in mind to put out, after that, a stamp depicting a fish, a sucker which might indicate that the general public was-the sucker. But instead of that they had a goat. There was some controversy about the art work of the design, but I suggested the government were using the public as a goat with regard to the increased rates charged.
This year they came up with a retriever, symbolic, perhaps, of the effort to retrieve the situation and restore the twice-a-day mail in the areas which had it before. The minister, in dealing with that subject the other day, said the cabinet was studying the matter, and there was quite a discussion about areas which do not have even one delivery a day. At the time when the twice-a-day delivery in urban areas was withdrawn the decision was, I presume, based on the fact that there was a shortage of manpower, and it was contended, I presume, that an effort should be made to effect some economies in the department to try to make up for diminishing returns, though in the future, when the manpower situation improved, and revenue improved, a return would be made to the twice-a-day delivery in the urban areas. Now we find that the situation is being reviewed. It seems to me a kind of situation where one service is being pitted against the other, the rural against the urban, and that is a situation that should not be.
If the government, or the department, in withdrawing the twice daily delivery from the urban areas, had expanded one-a-day service in the rural areas and given them an improved delivery the position would, I think, have been quite satisfactory. But this it did not do. The department chose to withdraw one delivery from the urban areas without in any way improving rural deliveries, and now it looks as though the urban areas are asking for the return of what they had before, and that this must now be done at the expense of the rural areas. I want to emphasize that in my opinion, in the light of the rates that are being imposed, there should be an improved delivery to the rural areas, particularly to those areas which are receiving only one delivery every two or three days, and the department should not make this competitive between urban and rural communities. The government should do something more substantial about this than it has done so far, instead of saying it is studying, on an economic basis, the possibility of returning to a two-a-day service.

Supply-Post Office
Revenue figures show that there has been an increase. I should like to refer now to what the hon. member for York-Scarborough said last week. I thought at the time, and I mentioned to the Postmaster General then that this was a liberal heresy for a member of the Liberal party to express, that post office salaries were not liberal enough-not enough for the employees to live on. The minister replied by saying that this matter was under the control of the civil service commission which had the task of studying the wages paid as compared with those paid by other industries. I would like to ask the minister if this question is at present before the civil service commission in any way at all. Is the commission studying the matter of an increase in wages to postal employees?
In the course of my remarks I tied up this question of the low salaries paid to postal employees with the pensions received by members of the staff who are drawing pensions. If those earning salaries are not getting enough to live on, then surely all pensioners are entitled to receive more than the pension they are getting. But the question now is, is anything being done about the men in the postal service?
I will leave this matter now, but I would point out once again that in my view the department should do something about improving service in the rural sections before introducing improvements in the urban sections, instead of playing one against the other, and it seems now that they are taking advantage of increased revenue without doing anything further.
Now at page 3 of the Postmaster General's report we find the following paragraph under "Purchasing and Stores":
During the year several changes were made in the scheduling of purchases to permit production by manufacturers during the months when there is a seasonal lull in employment. Advanced planning permits a greater volume of manufactured goods to be manufactured during the winter months. This is in accordance with a cabinet directive on winter employment.
Surely there is something wrong with the department's thinking if it has to wait on a directive of the cabinet telling them to place their orders at a time when industry is slack. Surely they did not need a directive from the cabinet about it; I am quite sure the department is more efficient than that. It puts the cabinet in a very sorry light, for this should have been a common practice over the years, and not have come to light at the present time, and the light just dawned on the cabinet to augment winter employment.
There was one thing that stood out in the Woods-Gordon report in regard to what they call time studies. The report gave considerable examples of how improvements and

economies could be brought about in the department-worth-while savings, particularly in the sorting operation. It was pointed out how in certain metropolitan areas such as Toronto and Montreal, which are handling mail based on a rate of $1 per hour to employees, there could be a saving made of approximately, it stated, .085 cents. And with one million letters going through a department in a day it was estimated that would amount to something like $850 of saving each day which, over the year, would amount to a saving in one area alone of $250,000.
But they did admit that there would have to be new equipment installed to effect savings of this kind and also that recruits would have to be enlisted and trained in order to effect these changes and improvements in the department. When the minister replies he will probably give us the number of schools for recruits that have been established in order that these time studies may be made and whether it has been done generally throughout the country or just in certain areas. He might tell us what equipment has been procured to effect these savings because in the Woods-Gordon report it was indicated that very substantial savings would be made amounting to some $250,000 in Toronto and Montreal and in other large areas in proportion, and that would mean something. But it is not evident from the estimates or in the report of the department and I think it should be gone into.
Some two or three years ago, when the department was under the late Mr. Cote, the matter of new equipment was brought up, and the possibilities in the future of making savings were pointed out. I refer to the sorting equipment. One particular type of equipment was mentioned which was in the development stage and it was mentioned that it was going to cost somewhere in the neighbourhood of $1 million or more. The development of the equipment had proceeded so far and we did not find out whether it had been put in operation. When pieces of equipment are in the progress stage and you are developing them and trying to make improvements, the only way you can effect this is to put them into operation. You find the difficulties, the gimmicks and the "bugs" as they are called and they are removed. It is three years now since we were told about that equipment, and at that time the minister held out great promise for the future of that kind of equipment and the savings that it was going to effect. I should like the Postmaster General to elaborate on that a little more and tell us what has become of that equipment and whether it has turned out to be a dud or is going to be of any future benefit to the department.

The minister replied to the hon. member for Peterborough regarding what is called the television operation or the viewing galleries, as I call them. Last year I referred to them as peeping Toms. I do not know whether they have effected any savings or have paid for the cost of establishing them. But I thought that some difficulties would be met in trying to put them into operation. In fact, if the pictures taken were not very good the department would probably have to call for a retake and would have to establish a board to decide if the operation was effective and the pictures good enough. They might get to the stage where these peeping Toms would probably be called all-seeing eyes. The Postmaster General would probably form an organization or association within the department and they would give him a button with the all-seeing eye on it. His subordinate officers would have spy glasses insignia as they would be of lesser rank in the organization. They would be using their spy glasses to watch what was going on in the postal department, and eventually the thing would become a joke throughout the country and the all-seeing eye or viewing operation in the postal department would be abolished, which I think will eventually happen.
But the truth of the matter is that these viewing stations have been in operation for a good many years, although not on such a large scale as at Peterborough and other centres. Can the Postmaster General outline to us what savings have been made through the establishment of these viewing galleries or television machines for taking pictures and tell us what beneficial effect it had upon the postal department to warrant the department spending that kind of money?

Mr. Chairman, before I make any remarks there is one question I should like to ask the minister. Are there any cities, towns or large villages in Canada with less than 2,500 delivery points which are receiving letter carrier delivery?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, there are some, and I have no doubt it will please the hon. member to know that there are to be some more during the present year.

I am very glad to hear the minister say that, and I rather hope that certain towns in my constituency, namely, the town of Ingersoll, about which the minister and I have had some correspondence, and also the town of Tillsonburg, may be among those included. I understand that a survey of the town of Ingersoll was made very recently and that there are about 2,169 potential points of delivery. I am very glad to hear what the minister has said for the
Supply-Post Office
reason that since there apparently is to be such a substantial surplus in the Post Office Department this year amounting to $30 million, I believe the figure was-

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I think I made a correction on that point yesterday. I pointed out that the ultimate surplus would be nearer $6 million when the fiscal year was over. That does not give me as much leeway to extend this type of service which my hon. friend desires.

I am still glad to hear that, while the amount of the surplus is not going to be what we thought it would be, there will still be a surplus of about $6 million. We have heard a number of members recommend that two deliveries a day be extended to urban centres. If there is to be a surplus, albeit $6,000,000, it seems to me there would be much better service to the people of Canada generally if letter carrier delivery was extended in the form of once a day delivery in some of the larger towns that have between 2,000 and 2,500 points of call. In a lot of these large towns with populations between 5,000 and 6,000 there are a great many elderly, retired people who may have come from the farm or elsewhere and have settled in these towns. It is quite a chore for them to have to walk down to the post office every day and get their mail, particularly on the very cold days of winter and the very hot days of summer.
Rather than extend twice a day delivery service to large urban and metropolitan centres, it would seem to me that if the minister has a surplus letter carrier delivery might well be extended to some of these large towns that are on the border line. The minister has told us that 2,500 points of delivery is the rule of thumb but, as he has indicated this afternoon, in some cases there are less than that number. In some cases towns with fewer delivery points have letter carrier delivery and he has indicated that there may be some more. Again I say I am glad to hear it and I hope that the two towns in my constituency which I have mentioned will be included.
I think they should be included for this very cogent reason. On these estimates last year the minister was asked a question on this subject and he told us that the rule of thumb was that there had to be an income of $50,000 a year and about 8,000 persons. Both Ingersoll and Tillsonburg have revenues very close to $50,000 a year. As a matter of fact, according to the last figures I have, the town of Tillsonburg, although somewhat smaller than Ingersoll, had a revenue in excess of $50,000 a year. I gather from what the minister has said that the rule of thumb

Supply-Post Office
is somewhat elastic. It does not seem fair to me that towns in some parts of the country should have letter carrier delivery when they are on the border line and others should not. I think this surplus might well be used for the purpose of including all towns which are very close to having between 2,000 and 2,500 delivery points. I do not see why it should be considered in any way fair that a town in one part of the country should get it and not a town in another part.

I have a few brief comments to make this afternoon. I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton concerning the number of citizens on any particular road. Not many years ago there would be anywhere from three to six persons to the mile on any given road, whereas at the present time there may be only one or two. I believe that these people are as deserving of mail delivery as they were formerly when there were five or six people to the mile.
One could make comparisons along this line with the people living on municipal roads and receiving municipal services. For instance the municipalities try to accommodate all these' people within the municipality, regardless of whether there are six or eight people to the mile, with road accommodation. Even if there is only one person to the mile, he is as deserving of road accommodation as anyone else. I believe the department should accommodate as many citizens as possible with rural mail delivery. Generally speaking, the rural roads are plowed in the winter, and if there are only two or three people to the mile they deserve the accommodation of rural mail delivery.
I have in mind one particular instance in my own constituency. At the time this rural route was inaugurated a farm at the end of the route was not occupied so the route stopped about three-quarters of a mile from this unoccupied farm. Since then the farm has been occupied and this man has been trying to get rural mail delivery but he has not been able to do so. I believe that particular citizen is entitled to rural mail delivery because if he had been living there at the time the route was inaugurated it would have been extended to his home. Why should he not receive that accommodation now? I hope to take this matter up with the Postmaster General or his assistant some time within the next week or two because that is one specific instance of an error caused by the fact the property was not occupied at the time the route was inaugurated. I say again that I believe the department should give every consideration to these citizens, just as

the municipalities give consideration to their citizens in providing them with service.
I have a few more comments to make, Mr. Chairman, with reference to salaries. I believe the salaries paid to rural mail carriers should be more uniform. There is a great variation between the salaries of mail carriers at the present time. I know that in my district there are mail carriers with fewer mail boxes on their routes who receive as large a salary or larger than some others with more extended routes. In fact, I have one specific case in mind. There are several fundamentals in connection with this case, so I will not embarrass the department by bringing it before the committee. This is another matter that I hope to take up with the minister or his assistant in the near future. I feel that there should be some schedule worked out whereby the salaries of the different mail carriers will be more uniform. I know of one particular case in which the rural mail carrier has not had an increase in his salary for many years, while other mail carriers working out of the same office have received one or two increases in their salaries. I feel that the one is no more deserving of it than the other. I say again, Mr. Chairman, I hope the department will work out some schedule whereby there will be more uniformity in the salaries of rural mail carriers.

About an hour or an hour and a half ago I informed the minister that I had received a communication from the postal employees relative to the fact they had not received their Christmas cheques. I have now had occasion to look back at the letter and I find I was also requested, in the same communication from the postal employees of Vancouver, to ask the minister an additional question. I am told that these employees are being exhorted by the income tax department to get their income tax returns in early. They inform me that not one of them has yet received their T-4 form from the government as to the deductions for income tax. They want to know just why it is that they are exhorted by one department to file their income tax returns early, and yet not one of them has received the necessary T-4 forms so that they can fill out their income tax form. The minister has told me the employees are receiving their Christmas cheques for overtime, but what about the forms?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
May I say with regard to the cheques to which my hon. friend referred that I have explained the cause of the delay. I am now informed that the cheques were sent out early this week and they should have arrived in Vancouver at the latest by yesterday.

With regard to the T-4 forms, again it is the same situation which I described previously. These forms have to be prepared by the central pay office and it is not until the figures are sent in by the district that the details are received to enable the T-4 form to be prepared. Furthermore, it is my understanding that these forms are sent to the local postmaster whose responsibility it is to add certain information such as marital status of the employee, his address and the amount of personal exemption to which he is entitled. This is done at the local office, so that it may take considerable time to add this information to the T-4 form.
I am further informed that this situation exists probably to a greater extent in the post office department than any other department because we do pay more overtime than other departments, and most of it is accumulated during one period of the year because of the increased volume of business at Christmas.
It is that much more complicated. I am told that the T-4 forms, which are those to which my hon. friend referred, for annual salary employees were made up by the central pay office on March 1. Therefore they are there and should be distributed by now.

May I ask my third, and I think my last question on this item? It is an important one and has been raised for many years. As far as my information is concerned, the situation is unchanged. The post office is perhaps one of the greatest exploiters of labour of any government department. I refer now to the policy which, according to my latest information, is still unchanged of employing year after year after year what is called temporary help. The department calls them temporary help but they work year after year. I have records of some of them going back to nine years. They are still classified as temporary help and they are paid a great deal less than if the department employed a proper and a full staff under proper salaries.
According to my information, there are still a great many employees in the Vancouver post office and in the districts who do work during the day and are employed at night. I understand that the number runs into approximately 300 overall. They are still classified as temporary help. The department must have their help. If my information from the minister's staff is correct, the department is exploiting labour by gypping labour through employing people under the name of temporary help no matter how long they are employed for. To my knowledge this matter has been raised for quite a number
Supply-Post Office
of years under these estimates. I have raised it myself every session under these estimates and I have yet to find any change.
I know the minister has two portfolios and is awfully busy. Can he say whether this matter is really under investigation now and that as speedily as possible these people will be employed on a permanent basis and not as temporary help? Under the present system the department is paying between 50 per cent and 60 per cent of the required wage instead of 100 per cent.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: This practice, Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member mentioned, has existed in the post office for many years, but I think the description which the hon. member gave was not exactly according to the facts. There is no question of exploiting or gypping the employees of the department. In all post offices -and I am told it exists elsewhere-there are peak periods when, for sortation purposes, you do need a certain number of increased personnel and just for a few hours.

Would the minister be prepared now to file answers and possibly give the names of all employees employed in the last 10 years in the Vancouver post office district, the hours, the days, the weeks, the months employed, and then tell me whether they are temporary employees?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think it has anything to do with what I am saying, and I can assure the hon. member that it would be rather difficult. If my hon. friend thinks it will serve a useful purpose I will get all the staff of the headquarters working to prepare such a list.
My point is that in every post office, particularly in those large post offices in the cities of Vancouver, Montreal and Toronto, there are peak hours when an increased number of people is necessary, and once that peak is over there is no more need for those people. They are needed over and above the normal establishment for a few hours every day. The practice in postal establishments has always been to take on people at a set rate for those hours. I can assure my hon. friend that, judging by the demands I have received from all over to get jobs, these temporary employees do not seem to consider that they are being gypped or exploited.
Will the Postmaster General tell us definitely whether he is going to bring down supplementary estimates later this year with respect to the year 1956-57?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows that my colleague, the Minister of Finance, is the one who brings down estimates and tables the supplementary estimates, as he does the main estimates. I am afraid he will have to

Supply-Post Office
direct his question to the Minister of Finance. I am not sure, Mr. Chairman, whether I would be in order to say whether I had asked for supplementary estimates or not. It is a matter completely outside of my jurisdiction as Postmaster General.

Mr. Chairman, I will admit immediately the phraseology of the question was rather unfortunate. Does the Postmaster General anticipate any requirement for funds in excess of those for 1956 of which we have already been advised?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman.
what amount?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No, I am afraid I cannot tell him that. That would be telling him what the supplementary estimates are and I am afraid I cannot do that.

It is
an interesting thing, Mr. Chairman,-

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wish to point out-and I am not trying to withhold information from my hon. friend-I think you will agree that it would not be in order for me as Postmaster General to tell the hon. member or the committee whether my colleague the Minister of Finance will be bringing down supplementary estimates for the year 1956-57 and to what amount. I am sure it would be out of order on my part to do so and that is the only reason why I am not giving the information he desires.

Mr. Chairman, I certainly do not want the Postmaster General to tell me what the Minister of Finance is going to do. We have had remarkably little success on this side of the house in finding that out but I do think that when we are discussing the estimates of his department for the coming year, and when he has presented certain figures to this house in those estimates, we are entitled to know, in order to pursue our discussions of the coming year a little further, as much as possible about the current year. The figures which we have before us at the present time lead one to believe that the department has a surplus of some $8,200,000 odd. The Postmaster General knows that the information which he gave the house on Friday was not quite as adequate as it should have been, although I sympathize with him because the conclusions which the press drew from it were ones which could easily be drawn. Since the information which he presented to the house enabled press gallery people to draw

wrong conclusions, he came back yesterday and explained and said, "My surplus is really going to be $6 million".
In the estimates before us we have $8,200,000. We have the Canadian press estimating it at $30 million. I am trying to get what the additional requirements are in respect of this year of which the committee has not yet been advised, which the Postmaster General knows about and which the Minister of Finance is going to tell us about. Certainly the Postmaster General is in a position to inform the committee as to what recommendation he is going to make to treasury board.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. Before that question is answered may I say that I am of the opinion it would be incorrect for any minister to state definitely before a recommendation has been received from His Excellency what that recommendation will be. wish I could hark back to the exact words of the debate of 1954 when the government proposed an increase in the postal rates of one cent on a letter. speechtext:
When the committee rose at six o'clock we had commenced to consider Bill No. 178, an act to amend the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act. I was about to call clause 1. I think I should draw the attention of the committee to the fact that in line 28 of clause 1 the words "in the opinion of the board" have been inserted by the committee on industrial relations between the words "until" and "the", so that the paragraph now reads:
Compensation is payable to an invalid child without regard to the age of such child, and payments to such child shall continue until, in the opinion of the board, the child ceases to be an invalid.
Clause 1, shall this clause carry?
On clause 1-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when second reading of this bill was being discussed I was called out of the chamber so before clause 1 carries I should like to commend the government for introducing this legislation at this time. This amendment is of considerable interest to my province, and particularly to my own riding, where so many people get their living from the sea. We all know that those who go down to the sea in ships live a very hazardous life. Every year the sea takes its toll and the number of widows and orphans of seamen in my province grows greater year by year. Of course, in a country like Canada, which depends so much on external trade, the merchant navy is the very lifeblood of our economy. It is extremely gratifying to me to see that measures are being taken to make better provision for the dependents of the deceased seamen.
There are one or two questions which I should like to ask the minister which he might answer at the appropriate time. I looked up the definition of "seaman" in the act and I found that it does not include fishermen. There are times when a banking vessel, after fishing for eight months out of the year, does engage in the coastal trade for perhaps one or two months during the slack season.

First of all, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I am gratified that the minister has seen fit to make the small amendment in the act as he has. I thought, while it may have been understood, nevertheless it was just as well that the act specifically set out that particular qualification. Really, there is not much to be said about this amending bill because it pretty well speaks for itself. It brings the compensation for merchant seamen, generally speaking, up to the average of compensation paid for workmen in other classifications across Canada. We are quite satisfied with the provisions in that regard.
There were one or two things that came out in committee that probably we would like to place on the record in this house. The first one is the protection for non-pilots which was stressed by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert. No doubt, he will say a few words about that. The other point I should like to mention particularly is the provision of rehabilitation services which are not specifically covered in the act and which are pretty much left, I would think, to the discretion of the board to arrange under the auspices of the rehabilitation service of the department. I trust that the officials who administer the act will see that in no case is an injured workman deprived of the necessary rehabilitation services. In my

opinion this is a matter that might very easily be overlooked once his medical and hospital expenses had been covered. I am sure that by stressing the point it will just draw it to the attention of those who are in charge of the administration of this act, and they will make sure that no one is deprived of this service. Possibly the big difficulty to be faced here is the fact that there are so few people who are actually served by this act that we may overlook the rather obvious services which might be made available to them. I think it is wise, for that reason, to mention these particular points.
In general, we are in accord with the provisions of the bill, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: INCREASED BENEFITS AND AMENDMENTS TO ADMINISTRATIVE PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I join with others in saying nothing about the bill. There is very little left to be said. It is an indication of considerable progress since 1946.
In the matter of rates the bill is better than the legislation of some of the provinces, and that is also true with respect to the dependents of deceased people who may have come under the act.
With regard to rehabilitation, very few of the provinces which have compensation acts are doing anything about rehabilitation. A person is placed on compensation. He is paid a certain rate while he is totally disabled from continuing his employment. After his period of treatment is over he is carried on compensation for a time and then he is taken before his doctor who decides that the person is 50 per cent better, and the compensation is cut 50 per cent. The doctor recommends light work in heavy industry where there is no light work. Therefore, during the period of rehabilitation the individual is eking out an existence on half compensation. Whether this act will work or not remains to be seen. Of course, you will not have the type of people to handle under this act that you would have in heavy industry.
I would like the minister to explain one thing. In most of the compensation acts across the country there is a provision having to do with occupational diseases, diseases that are peculiar to certain industries. I am wondering whether in this act any consideration has been given to that angle. Are there diseases peculiar to those engaged in the merchant service or in the occupation of seamen generally? Personally, I am quite satisfied with the act. I think we have made a lot of progress in a short time compared with the length of time it took us in most of the provinces to convince the government and the employers that we needed legislation of this kind.

The only thing I would like the minister to clear up is the matter of occupational diseases. Has the administration run into anything of that nature? I imagine that a person serving on salt water for a long period of time would be prone or susceptible to bronchial diseases. The minister might comment on that when he makes his remarks.

subtopic: INCREASED BENEFITS AND AMENDMENTS TO ADMINISTRATIVE PROVISIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on second reading and in committee we discussed the fact that there were still some seamen who did not come under the provisions of this act. I refer specifically to those in our pilotage service who are non-pilots. It was agreed that the intention of the act would be to include all seamen who did not come under compensation of a provincial or other governmental nature. Therefore, we should make certain that all seamen are looked after. We were given the assurance of the minister and the department at the time that these nonpilots would receive every consideration, and if it was ascertained that they would not benefit from any other civil damages or from the other benefits that might accrue through a legal court action the department would consider the plight of their dependents. I was quite satisfied with the treatment we gave to this subject but merely for the record here in committee I would like the minister simply to reiterate the statement he made that the department will seriously consider these nonpilots who were affected by the recent action in Saint John and that their dependents will be looked after in some way, as is the intention of this act.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: INCREASED BENEFITS AND AMENDMENTS TO ADMINISTRATIVE PROVISIONS

Mr. Chairman, may I refer to the point made on rehabilitation by both the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Hamilton West. While we have no direct facilities under this legislation to carry out rehabilitation services for those who are injured, nevertheless the very fact that the deputy minister of labour is the chairman of this board and has also under his responsibility the federal end of the vocational and technical training plan in conjunction with the provinces will make it very difficult for a case that may be subject to rehabilitation to be overlooked. I can assure both hon. members that that will be watched carefully.
Now, as to the other point raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, I think he should be the last person to say that the deep blue sea causes occupational diseases. I think it strengthens people rather than weakens them; but I think I will cover his point when I say that occupational hazards are certainly taken care of. He will recall
Supply-Northern Affairs that we started to name some of those hazards in the committee. They consisted of such things as getting tangled up in the hawser and slipping on a slippery deck. One unique case was that of a man who had lost his boat. He had climbed a tree to see where it was and fell out of the tree. These were certainly occupational hazards and the board decided that he was acting in the performance of his duty in trying to get back.
I am quite sure I am right in saying that those who are employed at this work-and I am sure the hon. member for Saint John-Albert will confirm this-are subject to no more occupational diseases than members of parliament, for instance.
With respect to the other point made by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, I will affirm here what I said at the committee stage. In conjunction with the Department of Transport and the Department of Justice we shall do our utmost to see that those pilots' assistants who unfortunately lost their lives in the accident in Saint John harbour and those who may suffer similar accidents will be favourably considered. If it is possible to do it we shall bring their dependents under this legislation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The estimates were introduced on February 22 by the minister and at that time he spoke very briefly, I think for about five minutes. What he had to say was only a listing of the projects and the amounts that these were expected to cost. No doubt he will elaborate on a considerable number of the projects as we proceed with our discussion of the estimates.
However, on the basis of what the minister said at that time I might point out I am glad to note that three-quarters of the increase in the estimates of the department for this year is slated for northern development. For several years past I have been urging on the minister and the government that a great deal more should be done as far as the development of our northland is concerned. I have been pleased to see that during the past two years the government has apparently become aware of the fact there is a very large field of development to be pursued in the north and has been appropriating larger sums each year for that development.
I think it is wise that the government has seen fit to appropriate $2J million this year for a road up to Yellowknife. I should like to have the minister tell us when he offers a reply what portion of that road is going to be built this year and how far the present contemplated appropriation of $2J million will take that road. In other words, I should like to know what proportion of the total length of the road it is intended that this expenditure will cover.
I was also glad to have the minister mention the provision for the first time of an appropriation to assist the provinces in the prevention of forest fires and for forest fire

protection generally. I understand that an amount of $500,000 is to be expended in this field. This is something for which the federal government should have been taking some responsibility a long time before this. The federal government did of course do something along this line in the forest conservation scheme on the eastern slope of the Rockies. To a large extent this was a forest fire prevention and control scheme but to my knowledge they have done nothing else along that line and I am extremely glad to learn that they are now entering this field.
The minister also mentioned that a special effort is to be made this year by the travel bureau to increase travel to the maritime provinces. I think this policy will be welcomed by everyone. The general activities of the travel bureau have been relatively successful although they have been limited in what they could do by the amount of money appropriated to them. I think it is a good thing that they are featuring in their advertisements and publicity one particular part of Canada each year with a view to increasing tourist trade. I would think this policy will prove more effective than general advertisements designed to attract tourists to Canada. The highlighting of a specific area in Canada each year is a worthwhile innovation and I trust it will be successful in attracting a greatly increased number of tourists to the Atlantic provinces during the coming year.
Before I proceed with the remarks I intended to make I would like to pay tribute to the officers of this department and particularly the officials of the northern affairs branch who are dedicated men doing an extremely worth-while job. By singling out the officers in the northern affairs branch I do not mean to cast any reflection on the officials of any other branch-and there are many branches in this department-because almost without exception the officials with whom I have come in contact have commanded my respect and admiration.
I should like to open my general remarks on these estimates, Mr. Chairman, by quoting from a speech which was made by Professor Creighton in Ottawa on February 16, as reported in the Ottawa Journal of February 18. The report reads in part:
Professor Creighton reviewed Macdonald's achievement

That is of course a reference to Sir John A. Macdonald.
-in bringing about confederation on the assumption that Canada was economically viable in its own right and could be organized as a separate and competitive economy in North America.
Canada today had a second chance to prove Laurier's claim that the twentieth century belonged to her. The northwest gave the nation a boom

in the first half of the century and now the northwest offered new riches in metals, fuels and sources of energy and power. How they would be developed and used would, in all probability, depend the entire future history of Canada.
Those remarks are profoundly true in my opinion. The first great rapid surge of population and development in this country came as a result of the opening up of the west following the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway. As Professor Creighton points out, we now have at our feet a second great phase of development in the north. The development of the resources of the north of course includes the northern parts of the provinces as well as the Yukon and Northwest Territories. As far as the provinces are concerned, individually they have the primary responsibility for the development of those areas although the dominion government also has a responsibility to assist them to put into effect policies which will enable the development of the northern regions of the provinces to proceed satisfactorily.
With regard to the Yukon and Northwest Territories the sole responsibility rests with the central government and particularly the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
There are, I think, two main keys to making this development possible and to making the resources of those northern areas available to the people of Canada. The first of these is, of course, transportation.
The department has finally recognized that this is the case. For some considerable time- up until last summer, as a matter of fact- everything that was said by members who came from the north and by others of us who were interested in that northern development and had it at heart was fairly well pooh-poohed by the department and the government or at least nothing was done about it. But as I say, the department has now recognized the fact that transportation into these northern areas is absolutely vital and necessary if their development is to take place.
I placed on the record last year-and I should like to do so again-a few excerpts from a brief presented to the Gordon commission by Mr. Robertson, the deputy minister of this department, with regard to the Northwest Territories. At page 19 of that brief we find these words:
The most difficult and urgent problem to be faced in the economic development of the Northwest Territories is transportation.
As I say, this fact has finally been realized by the department. Following that there are various other quotations which emphasize and re-emphasize the necessity for the provision of better transportation into these
Supply-Northern Affairs areas if the resources of the areas are to be economically and profitably developed. What I wonder, however, is whether the government as a whole has yet recognized what the facts are in this connection and whether it is prepared to go ahead in an energetic way to provide the means of transportation which are essential for the development of that area.
In this same brief at page 24 we find these words:
[DOT]	[DOT]	. three methods by which transportation
facilities into the Northwest Territories might be improved. The first is the construction of a railroad to Great Slave lake.
I have failed to find in the estimates anything to indicate that the government is taking any steps to initiate a railway to Great Slave lake. Perhaps the minister may be able to tell us at a later time that something is being done in this regard. I certainly trust so. But as I say, a perusal of the estimates did not indicate that the government is giving any consideration, this year at least, to the provision of that railway which the department itself in its brief has indicated is essential. Then the quotation continues:
The second is the construction of roads into promising resource development areas when and as indications suggest that these areas, given highway transportation, would be economic to develop.
The road which I mentioned earlier and which the minister stated was going to have $2J million spent on it this year to Yellowknife is of course a road of that type. I am only sorry that there are not other roads, particularly roads extending into the area beyond Yellowknife, which are provided for in any of this year's estimates.

speechtext: There was some provision last year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
What was provided for last year was an extremely limited program which extended a very few miles from Yellowknife and quite failed, I think, to meet the necessities of the situation which exist there. The quotation continues:
The third is the adoption of a policy of supplying the newly constructed defence stations in the Northwest Territories by commercial air services and the establishment of a network of scheduled commercial air lines in the Arctic.
In spite of the fact that this apparently is the general idea of the department, in actual practice the reverse seems to be the case. Air lines which wish to establish scheduled air services into the north have been discouraged and in effect have been prevented from establishing those scheduled air routes into that northern country.
I would point out that in addition to removing that road block to independent

Supply-Northern Affairs private air lines establishing routes into the north, there is a necessity for considerably more to be done in the provision of air landing strips. As far as the far north, the extreme Arctic, is concerned, a great many air landing strips have been provided through the Construction of the D.E.W. line stations. In the areas farther south, however, where a considerable amount of scrub exists in places, considerable forested areas and so on, much less has been done. Those are the areas to quite an extent where the greatest resource development may be expected to take place and where the provision of landing strips in considerably increased numbers is essential.
I said that in my opinion the first great key to unlocking the resources of the north is transportation. The second great key I believe is the harnessing of the hydroelectric power of the rivers of this country, particularly those in the north. In this regard I refer particularly to the water power of the Columbia river in British Columbia and of the Yukon river. This whole matter of the development of the water power of these two rivers is now under consideration by the Canadian and United States governments.
In this connection I should like to read briefly from an article by Bruce Hutchison in Maclean's magazine of November 29, 1956, in which he deals with this question of the Columbia river particularly and also the Yukon river and the hydroelectric possibilities of those two rivers. The article is entitled "The Coming Battle for the Columbia". These are the words that I should particularly like to bring to the attention of the committee:
Early next year the two friendly neighbours will begin their most important negotiations since the abortive reciprocity agreement of 1911; Canada seems to hold all the aces in a gigantic poker game of diplomacy. The U.S. is apparently hoist on two separate petards of its own making and ruefully confronts two errors impelled by its lack of foresight.
Nevertheless, the bargain now in the making, though it holds immense opportunities for Canada, presents dangers of equal magnitude. That question-far more significant than most of the partisan issues now convulsing domestic Canadian politics- will be answered in the next year or two.
Then down a little bit further he goes on to say this:
The agenda of Canadian politics contains many impressive items, soon to receive the verdict of the electors. All of them-even the controversial gas pipe line-are dwarfed in importance by the management, or mismanagement, of the Columbia.
Then he goes on to point out what the immense hydroelectric potential of that river is. He points out that all of the rivers of North America are estimated to contain a fifth of the hydroelectric power of the world and that the Columbia is estimated to contain
[Mr. Harkness.l
a third of that fifth, or in other words a third of the hydroelectric power of the continent. The article of course goes on to point out what the legal position is and to express the fear that, in spite of the fact that on legal grounds Canada would seem to be in a position of having complete control of what is done on the waters of the Columbia river and on the waters of the Yukon river, nevertheless the pressure of the United States, much larger than ourselves and upon whom we are dependent as far as defence matters are concerned, and so forth, may be such as to cause our government in effect to give away a considerable number of our rights.
I would like the minister, when he comes to reply to the speeches made here, to indicate to the house what the situation is with regard to the negotiations concerning the use of the water power of the Columbia and the Yukon rivers, and to give an assurance to the house that Canada will not be "sold down the river" with regard to its hydroelectric resources. The whole tenor of this article is that that is the greatest danger facing Canada from an economic point of view at the present time, and I think that in view, particularly, of the considerable amount of speculation there has been about this matter and in view of the numerous statements which have been made in the United States in connection with it, the government, through its ministers, owes it to the house and to the people of Canada to make a definite statement in regard to the Columbia and the Yukon river waters, and to say that Canada is going to maintain its rights in connection with those waters.
There was another matter on which I spoke at considerable length last year, I will mention it only briefly now: that is, the D.E.W. line stations in our far north. Last year I pointed out that a considerable number of newspapermen who had been on a trip up in that area had written articles indicating that to a considerable extent the far north had been alienated to the American air force personnel who were, in many cases, in charge of the air stations being constructed in the north. This view was expressed in another article in Maclean's by Ralph Allen, in this case in an article on May 26. He stated the position in this form:
The suggestion that Canada is only the nominal ruler of this important part of Canada and that the United States is the real ruler is not taken seriously anywhere except on the DEW line itself. There, the truth is palpable and inescapable.
And a little further on in the article, he said:
The most experienced and responsible Canadian I met in the north was a man X would rather not identify more closely than that. I asked him bluntly:	"Do you and your friends resent the

presence of the Americans here?" "No," he said sadly. "It is the other way round. They resent our presence here."
As I say, I spoke on this at some considerable length last year, and the minister did not give any satisfactory replies or assurance in this matter. I urged him that, in order to demonstrate the fact that this was Canadian territory, we should actively exercise sovereignty over it in all parts, and that there should be some representative of the civil power, a mounted police officer or a representative of the minister's department at every one of these D. E. W. line stations rather than the situation which existed at that time, last year, at least, when there was one mounted policeman at each of the main stations, and three or four stations between these main stations would be without any representative. I hope a change has taken place in that situation since last year. I would like the minister to tell us what the situation is at the present time, and what has been done in regard to the matter.
Along the same lines, we had quite a discussion last year in regard to how far north of the Canadian mainland Canadian sovereignty extended, and the hon. member for York West pointed out that booklets put out by the various Canadian departments showed our northland extending in a segment right up to the north pole. The minister completely "pooh-poohed" that idea, and said "No, no, that is only floating ice; we have no sovereignty over it, no control", and so forth. The point was brought up, as a matter of fact, because of reports current last year that the Russians had weather stations and similar installations on some of this ice. We pointed out that whether it was floating ice in all cases or whether some of it was land, nobody knew; it was impossible to determine that, and nobody had been there to survey it. In any event this "segment" principle had been enunciated many years before and we were very surprised, when the question happened to come up, that the minister disavowed it, although it had been maintained by a former minister of the interior.
